As a heads up this is the sort of conversation that's going to bring out emotions in people, even perfectly qualified people. Take everything you read, obviously including whatever I write, with a grain of salt.

Programming is abstraction. Taking one concept and making it somewhat more intuitive. If you start at the lowest human usable level you have assembly language:

mov ah,2
mov dl,7
int 21
int 20

Each of those instructions translates directly into binary sequence. mov ah,2 might be 0000111100010001. Those bits are glued together and that's exactly what is sent to your processor. In the old school days of DOS that would be the source code for an entire program that would make nice annoying BEEP sound and then exit.

C abstracts that away. Instead now you might have:

main(int, char*)
{
 printf("\a");
}

Identical program and is obviously a huge step forward in abstracting away stuff. The \a standing for "alarm." Well at least it's identical in functionality. In reality the executable for that code is going to be vastly more complex and feature an enormous amount of boiler plate. The language is designed for practical use, not making beep.com.

Now we enter C++. The big difference between C++ and C is the introduction of an abstraction of "objects." Let's say you're writing a program to draw a bunch of shapes. In C you might have a bunch of different functions DrawSquare, DrawTriangle, DrawCircle. In C++ you could abstract this away and actually treat the shapes as a single entity. So for instance you might have something like:

Shape* shapes = new Shape[3];
shapes[0] = new Square();
shapes[1] = new Triangle();
shapes[2] = new Circle();
for( int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
 shapes[i].DrawMe()

The cool thing about objects is that it makes conceptualizing any program much more logical. If you're making a game you might have a world and within that world is a list of objects. As long as you implement a certain required level of functionality, an object can be called a shape. And then you could have things like the ability to automatically render any shape, or change its location, or give it a lifebar or an AI update system, and so forth.

Now the next step, up to C#, is a bit unusual. I would actually call the early incarnations of C# as a cleaner implementation of C++. C++ is not a friendly language. This isn't a matter of competence either. Any programmer, regardless of their skill level, is going to spend an inordinate amount of their time trying to figure out why things aren't working like they thought they would. Memory issues are one of many examples here. Imagine you have a buffer that has just enough memory to hold the word "hello" - 5 bytes. Now through one of the infinite possible ways of doing so you end up accidentally writing to the 6th byte of this buffer. In C/C++ this is often times completely legal, as is the opposite. As a brief aside, the well known HeartBleed bug was actually incredibly trivial. It was little more than reading more than the bounds of an array. Instead of reading 5 bytes for hello, you read 50,000 bytes. The important thing is that what comes after the data you intended to write or read from is also going to frequently be data. When you write to the 6th byte of that array you might have suddenly changed a value that has nothing whatsoever to do with that string. It could be something used in an entirely different context. So when you're tracking down the bug what you're going to see is that other variable getting a strange value. Perhaps even worse is when it doesn't actually critically cripple your application. It instead is just one of those seemingly irreconcilable glitches. Everything works fine until the 0.01% when it doesn't and suddenly your program keeps operating but produces critically incorrect output. I have no doubt cumulatively millions of hours of programmer manpower have been spent tracking down bugs just like this.

C# aimed to and succeeded in cleaning this up. Bounds checks verification is enabled by default, automated memory management is enabled by default, and so forth. This is already huge. But where C# really shines is where it went after it'd provided what I'd call "clean C++." The problem here is that most of these features are fairly advanced and so I don't think they're necessarily appropriate here. Me talking about the cool things you can do with lambdas, the task parallel library, built in super clean asynchronous operations, runtime reflection (and compilation!), lazy exection and LINQ fun, and way more than I think of off the top of my head as I'm passing out while writing this. On that note this is probably becoming somewhat of a novel. The point being that it started out as clean C++ then started piling on great features. In fact the most recent updates to C++ have been in large part playing catchup to C#. The one negative to C# was performance. Particularly in its very early stages C# had performance issues. Those issues are gone.

I'd recommend starting at the bottom and working your way up if you wish to develop a sound foundation. Between C++ and C# I would recommend C++ first. While you can always do more the higher you go up the chain, understanding the implications -performance, memory, and so on- of what you're actually doing and how it's likely implemented behind the scenes is crucial for developing a sound intuitive foundation to work from.

In C you might have a bunch of different functions DrawSquare, DrawTriangle, DrawCircle.

I would like to add emphasis to the fact that this pattern is only one out of many ways to approach the problem of drawing shapes in C, and that it is not something fundamental to the design of the C language.

Another common option in C would be to define a pure function which returns the next shape value in a sequence of shapes as a union or struct on the stack, or to define a procedure which writes out a sequence of shapes as structs or unions to a typed pointer.

Under such a data-driven approach, you could then let the main loop of your program maintain control and call these functions to infer the correct output to generate, without having to define an additional imperative API to call into and interrupt it with additional information.
